also: give me a moment to think

evidence: Sen. Ep. 63.2: etiam Niobam dē cibō cōgitāsse
Cic. Off. 1.105: mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō
terms.comment: With dē and the ablative for what one thinks about (dē tē cōgitō), an accusative, or a question (quid agam cōgitō). With an infinitive it means “intend” (see mean, intend).

evidence: Ter. Eun. 592: Dum haec mēcum reputō
terms.comment: Mostly with sēcum or cum animō: turning something over in one’s mind.

phrases.latin: aedificāre diū cōgitāre oportet, cōnserere cōgitāre nōn oportet, sed facere oportet
phrases.english: Building you should think about for a long time; planting you shouldn’t think about: you should just do it.

phrases.latin: cum dīxerit etiam Niobam dē cibō cōgitāsse
phrases.english: since Homer said that even Niobe thought about food
Let me think for a moment.

phrases.latin: sed quid est, Palaestriō, quod volūtās tūte tēcum in corde? — Paulisper tacē, dum ego mihi cōnsilia in animum convocō et dum cōnsulō quid agam
phrases.english: But what is it, Palaestrio, that you’re turning over in your heart? — Be quiet a moment, while I call my plans together and think what to do

phrases.latin: Quamobrem, cum diūtule tacitus in cōgitandō fuissem, respondī tandem nōn vidērī mihi significārī eam rem posse ūnō nōmine
phrases.english: So, after thinking a little while in silence, I answered at last that I did not think the thing could be expressed in one word

sources: Lewis & Short: cogito · Lewis & Short: reputo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 109, 393.
